newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Chiroscience braced for key year.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Chiroscience braced for key year.

text.p: Britain's Chiroscience Group Plc announced a sharp rise in full-year losses on Monday as it geared up for a key year in the development of its busy pipeline of new drugs.

Pre-tax losses at the nine-year old biotech company widened to 18.7 million pounds ($30.4 million) from 11.64 million in the year ended February 28, largely reflecting an 84 percent rise in research and development spending to 22.2 million pounds.

Chiroscience was also able to report the first-ever operating profit at its technical services arm, which helps other drug companies with research, and a 113 percent jump in revenues to 11.5 million pounds.

But the company told Reuters that spending was likely to outstrip income by around 2 million pounds every month this year as it prepared to launch an important new local anaesthetic, Levobupivacaine, and readied novel drugs for cancer and asthma for clinical trials.
"This year is clearly going to be very important. Levobupivacaine is a key milestone for the company and we are totally focused on that," chief executive John Padfield said.
Analysts said Levobupivacaine, currently undergoing 20 separate late-stage trials, would provide crucial funding for the rest of Chiroscience's pipeline.
With an increasing trend towards cheaper day surgery boosting the market for long-acting anaesthetics, analysts at Lehman Brothers forecast $250 million of sales for the Chiroscience product by 2003.
But despite Padfield's confidence that the anaesthetic would be ready for approval by European regulators in December, shares in Chiroscience drifted down 10 pence to 342-1/2 after the results.

The stock is well below a brief high of 587 pence touched in April 1996, since when Chiroscience has underperformed the FT-SE All Share index by more than seven percent and the Pharmaceutical index by nearly six percent, according to Reuters 3000 data.

Analysts said the market was waiting for news of high-profile partnerships for Chiroscience's major products and for more detail about the U.S. gene-research company, Darwin Molecular, which Chiroscience bought for $120 million last December.

Padfield told Reuters that an update on Chiroscience's technology platform including Darwin would be given to investors on May 30. He also said the company was in talks with several companies about marketing Levobupivacaine, a purified version of an existing anaesthetic which appears to have much lower side effects than the original.
But he indicated that he would take a case-by-case approach for partnerships on the pipeline of more novel drugs.
With an asthma compound expected to start clinical trials next month, Padfield said a company with a strong track record in the highly competitive asthma field would be attractive.
"There are some very established players and you are talking about very expensive clinical trials to get this to the market," Padfield said.

However, in the area of MMP inhibitors, a new class of drugs which includes British Biotech Plc cancer treatment Marimastat, Padfield said British Biotech had shown it was "possible to take this on further without massive investment."
Two MMP inhibitor drugs, which suppress an enzyme that is crucial for cancer's spread through the body, are due to begin human trials by the end of 1997.

Although the British Biotech approach of going it alone on cancer would allow Chiroscience to keep a bigger chunk of the rewards from a successful drug, it could also force the company to go back to shareholders for more cash.
"But we would only do that if there was a very good story to tell," said finance director Christine Soden.
